title: Touching Materials Visually: About the Dominance of Vision in Building Material Assessment
central_proposition: Vision dominates the assessment of building materials by architecture students, often leading to a disregard for tactile properties and an inability to correctly identify materials by touch alone, highlighting a need for more elaborate consideration of non-visual aspects in design education.

concept_definitions.name: Visual focus in architecture
concept_definitions.definition: Architects' tendency to prioritize visual aspects in design, potentially disregarding non-visual aspects, often considered a strength in design research but increasingly criticized in architecture.

concept_definitions.name: Multisensory assessment
concept_definitions.definition: Evaluation of materials involving multiple senses (e.g., vision and touch) to anticipate people's experiences.

concept_definitions.name: Experiential qualities
concept_definitions.definition: Properties of materials that evoke sensory experiences (e.g., warmth, roughness, gloss) and contribute to the perception of architectural space.

argument_structure: The paper presents an empirical study comparing visual-only, touch-only, and multisensory (vision and touch) assessment of building materials by architecture students. It analyzes quantitative attribute ratings and qualitative keyword associations to demonstrate the dominance of vision and the differences in perception across sensory modalities. The discussion then interprets these findings to argue for a more multisensory approach in architectural design and education.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Visual information leads to more cognitive interpretations and overrides actual physical/sensory observations, especially for attributes like warmth, where visual cues (e.g., color) and associated meanings (e.g., concrete is cold) take precedence over tactile sensations. The identification of materials by touch alone is more difficult than by vision, and tactile cues are disregarded when vision is available, suggesting a hierarchical processing where vision gates or overrides other sensory inputs.

findings.antecedent: Years of architectural education (beyond first year)
findings.consequent: Assessment of material attributes (pleasant, hard, flat)
findings.mechanism: The influence of architectural education on basic perceptual judgments of materials largely stabilizes after the first year, indicating a limited evolution of sensory assessment skills during training.
findings.source: Years of Education versus Material Assessment
findings.quote: the years of architectural education hardly affected the participants' assessment of building materials concerning the attributes under study.
findings.empirical_support_cited: ANOVA results showed no significant main effects of Education for most attributes (p > 0.05), except for first-year students rating materials flatter and harder.

findings.consequent: Assessment of material attributes (complex pattern, glossy, massive, warm)
findings.mechanism: Different sensory modalities pick up distinct cues; touch relies on surface texture and thermal properties, while vision integrates color, light, and visual patterns, leading to divergent perceptions of the same material properties.
findings.quote: The tactile assessment (TAC) of complex pattern, glossy, massive, and warm was significantly different (p ≤ 0.05) from the evaluations where participants used vision
findings.empirical_support_cited: Tactile assessment (TAC) of complex pattern, glossy, massive, and warm was significantly different (p ≤ 0.05) from vision-based evaluations (GEN and VIS).

findings.antecedent: Presence of vision in material assessment
findings.mechanism: Visual information, being the dominant sensory modality, overrides or disregards tactile input, leading to a perception that aligns with visual cues even when other senses are also engaged.
findings.quote: no significant differences between the general and visual evaluations of the materials (p > 0.05 for all attributes).
findings.empirical_support_cited: No significant differences were found between general (GEN) and visual (VIS) evaluations for any attributes (p > 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Reliance on touch only for material identification
findings.mechanism: Touch alone provides insufficient cues for accurate material identification compared to vision, which integrates more comprehensive information, especially regarding shape and overall appearance.
findings.quote: When participants relied on touch only (TAC), many material labels did not match the material being assessed.
findings.empirical_support_cited: When participants relied on touch only (TAC), many material labels did not match the material being assessed. Only steel was correctly identified.

findings.antecedent: Visual cues (e.g., cold grey color) and cognitive associations (e.g., concrete is cold)
findings.mechanism: Cognitive interpretations and visual parameters override actual tactile sensations, leading to a perceived warmth that aligns with visual and associative priors rather than direct physical properties.
findings.source: Tactile Evaluation Differs from Visual Evaluation
findings.quote: the cold grey color of concrete contributes to the perception of coldness during visual evaluation
findings.empirical_support_cited: Concrete was evaluated to be colder when using vision compared to using touch, with its cold grey color and associated meaning contributing to this perception.

findings.antecedent: Reliance on touch only (absence of vision)
findings.consequent: Frequency of material naming and technical/sensory descriptions
findings.mechanism: When visual information is unavailable, individuals compensate by actively seeking to identify materials and focusing more on direct physical and sensory properties to construct a mental representation.
findings.source: Naming materials; Technical and sensory descriptions
findings.quote: The test condition related significantly to the number of material labels named by the participants, X²(2) = 97.9, p < 0.001.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Material labels were used more in the tactile test condition (21.0%) than in general (4.8%) or visual (7.0%) conditions (X²(2) = 97.9, p < 0.001). Technical and sensory descriptions were also more frequent in tactile (43.9%) than other conditions (X²(2) = 53.8, p < 0.001).

findings.antecedent: Presence of vision in material assessment
findings.consequent: Frequency of expressive and associative meanings
findings.mechanism: Visual information facilitates cognitive interpretations and triggers personal experiences and associations, shifting the assessment from direct physical characteristics to broader, more abstract meanings.
findings.quote: A significant effect of the test condition was found, X²(2) = 86.5, p < 0.001.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Expressive and associative meanings were mentioned more frequently with vision (65.7% GEN, 69.3% VIS) than with touch only (34.6%) (X²(2) = 86.5, p < 0.001).

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Architectural students beyond their first year will show consistent assessments of material attributes (e.g., pleasantness, hardness, flatness) regardless of further educational training.
Tactile assessment of material attributes (e.g., pattern, gloss, massiveness, warmth) will significantly differ from visual or multisensory assessment due to distinct sensory cues.
In multisensory material assessment, visual input will dominate, leading to evaluations that are statistically indistinguishable from visual-only assessments for most attributes.
Reliance on touch alone will result in significantly lower accuracy in material identification compared to assessments involving vision.
Cognitive associations and visual cues (e.g., color) will override actual tactile sensations (e.g., warmth) in the overall perception of material properties.
The absence of visual information will lead to a compensatory increase in explicit material naming and descriptions of technical/sensory properties during assessment.

The presence of visual information will significantly increase the generation of expressive and associative meanings related to materials, reflecting a shift towards cognitive interpretations over direct sensory impressions.
bridge_warrants: The findings align with dual-process theories, where visual information triggers more cognitive interpretations and overrides direct sensory impressions.
The study contributes to multisensory integration frameworks by demonstrating visual dominance and compensatory processing when visual cues are absent.

The results suggest that expertise (years of education) does not significantly alter fundamental sensory biases in material assessment, linking to discussions on the development of professional perception.
methodological_critiques: The use of small-scale material samples may not fully represent real-life architectural settings or full-scale walls.
The study focused only on vision versus touch, and future research should include all senses (auditory, olfactory) for a comprehensive understanding.
The experimental setup, while controlled, may not fully capture the complexity of architects' real-life material selection processes for specific projects.
model_structure: The paper implicitly suggests a hierarchical model of sensory processing in material assessment, where visual input typically holds a dominant position, influencing or overriding information from other modalities like touch. When vision is absent, compensatory mechanisms engage, leading to increased reliance on and explicit description of available sensory cues.
limitations: The study used small-scale samples (0.4m x 0.4m), which may not fully represent full-scale walls.
The focus was limited to indoor wall applications.
The study primarily investigated vision versus touch, and other senses (auditory, olfactory) were not explicitly varied.
The experimental setup may not fully reflect the real-life material selection process of architects for specific projects.

paper_metadata.title: Emotional Behaviors, Emotivational Goals, Emotion Strategies: Multiple Levels of Organization Integrate Variable and Consistent Responses
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Emotional Behaviors, Emotivational Goals, Emotion Strategies: Multiple Levels of Organization Integrate Variable and Consistent Responses
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Researchers have found undeniable variability and irrefutable evidence of consistencies in emotional responses across situations, individuals, and cultures. Both must be acknowledged in constructing adequate, enduring models of emotional phenomena. In this article I outline an empirically-grounded model of the structure of the emotion system, in which relatively variable actions may be used to pursue relatively consistent goals within discrete emotion syndromes; the syndromes form a stable, coherent set of strategies for coping with crises and opportunities. I also discuss a framework that can integrate dimensional and discrete perspectives on emotions.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: In the assessment of material attributes, visual information often dominates or overrides information from other sensory modalities, particularly touch.
Years of specialized training, such as architectural education, lead to the development of distinct perceptual strategies and sensitivities for material assessment.

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural education fosters specific cognitive frameworks and perceptual strategies that prioritize visual cues in the assessment of material attributes, leading to a visually-dominant material assessment.
